{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1→## Multivitamin Compliance Reduces Injuries of Female Recruits at Air Force Basic Training: A Randomized Controlled Cohort Study

Korey B. Kasper, MD, CAQSM *; Meredith Cockerell, MS,  ATC†; Clarissa Escamilla, MS, RDN, LD‡;

Richard Gonzalez, MDS, RDN, LD‡

## ABSTRACT

## Introduction:
10→
Department of the Air Force basic military training (BMT) is the 7.5-week initial entry training for all enlisting U.S. Air Force and Space Force recruits. Overuse musculoskeletal injuries (MSKI) during training threaten success in BMT, and trainees with nutritional deficiencies are at higher risk. Several efforts are made at BMT to mitigate these issues to help trainees graduate on time, such as the distribution of multivitamins (MVI) to female recruits. However, trainee compliance with the prescribed MVI has been reported to be low, calling into question the effectiveness of this intervention. This study evaluated the effect of briefing modality offered to these trainees at the time of distribution on educational effectiveness, MVI compliance, and injury rates.

## Materials and Methods:

This was a randomized controlled cohort study of BMT female trainees. Subjects included all female trainees of a single iteration of BMT concurrently completing training within the same squadron. At the outset of training, cohorts were randomly educated in one of two ways regarding the provided MVI. The control cohort ( n = 80) was presented with the standard educational video created by BMT-registered dietitians, while the test cohort ( n = 79) was presented the video and then also briefed in-person by a group of subject matter experts. At the end of BMT, the trainees completed a questionnaire regarding their knowledge, confidence, and compliance with the MVI. Additionally, a routinely collected training database was queried and analyzed for differences in injuries and training outcomes using the chi-squared test with significance set to α≤ 0.05.

## Results:

Although both cohorts found their educational presentation useful, the 'in-person' cohort reported significantly higher compliance rates and were found to be diagnosed with MSKI and bone stress injuries at significantly lower rates (43% and 66% relative risk reductions, respectively).
20→
## Conclusions:

Education to female BMT trainees regarding the MVI, which included a face-to-face discussion with subject matter experts,  resulted in greater compliance and reduced incidence of MSKI and bone stress injury, compared to a video prepared by registered dietitians alone. Such educational approaches should continue to be strived for in this and other military population health measures. This study's implication of MVI efficacy for injury risk reduction in female trainees should be further studied, verified, and improved upon in this and other populations.

## INTRODUCTION

Nutritional deficiency is common among military trainees 1-5 at  the  Department  of  the  Air  Force  basic  military training (BMT), the 7.5-week physically, mentally, and emotionally  demanding  initial  training  for  recruits  seeking enlistment  into  the  U.S.  Air  Force  and  U.S.  Space  Force. Deficiencies occurring before BMT (baseline nutrition) and during BMT (relative to training demands or in response to exercise and adaptations) can interfere with training success via effects on musculoskeletal injury (MSKI), 6 illness, 7-9 and poor mental and physical adaptation and performance. 4,10-19

Bone stress injury (BSI) is a specific overuse MSKI very common  in  military  recruits,  to  which  those  harboring  a nutritional deficiency are at higher risk. 20-23 In a recent publication, 13.87% of male trainees and 14.13% of female trainees were clinically diagnosed with BSI at BMT. 24 These conditions  result  in  increased  health  care  costs,  training  disruptions, delayed graduation ($384.33/day/trainee), and incompletion of training rates (

  "text": "--- Page 2 ---
its nutritional risk factors (such as low-energy availability, 26 iron, 5,22,27 and calcium/vitamin D 28,29 )  thus  present important targets for prevention and mitigation efforts in military training.
BSI-facilitating nutritional deficits in BMT trainees occur for  myriad  reasons  which  have  been  reported  clinically  by trainees  to  the  clinicians  of  this  authorship  team.  Before BMT, trainees may be affected by food insecurity, knowledge deficits, and restricted diets. During BMT, intake of adequate nutrition  may be hindered by unavailability of preferred or religious food choices at the dining facilities (DFAC), lack of adequate mealtime in the DFAC, and appetite reductions associated with the stress of training. Regardless of the reasons, trainees with intentional or unintentional nutritional deficits at BMT are predisposed to worse training adaptation, which may lead to hindered performance as well as MSKI; such trainees are at higher risk to not graduate BMT on time or at all. 30
For  these  reasons, BMT  has  taken  steps  to  improve the  fueling  of  trainees.  DFAC  food  product  offerings  have improved to  better  meet  nutritional  needs  and  specific  diet requirements of individuals.  Furthermore,  in BMT DFACs, changes to choice architecture and the introduction of the Go For Green® program, 31 which provides quick assessments of menu item nutritional value,  have  helped  direct  trainees  to healthier choices. Beyond their three daily meals in the DFAC, since 2012, trainees have been provided an evening snack in the form of their choice of a fruit or nutrition bar 'to improve nutritional adequacy and timing in relation to exercise and as well as reduce attrition.' 4
Female military trainees are at higher risk of nutritional deficiency,  most  notably  iron  deficiency, 5,32-34 injury, 23,30 and  attrition 35 compared  to  their  male  counterparts. To address  these  disproportionate  risks  and  'improve  performance and decrease rates of attrition,' a daily prenatal multivitamin (MVI) with iron has been prescribed and distributed to females arriving to BMT, since 2012. 35 Of note, this MVI is labeled 'prenatal' because of its folic acid content (which is  recommended  for  all  females  of  child-bearing  potential per  the  Centers  for  Disease  Control  and  Prevention 36 and the United States Preventive Services Task Force 37 ) and was chosen because prenatal MVIs are on the organization's formulary whereas other MVIs are not. However, the MVI was chosen specifically for vitamin D and iron supplementation. The contents of this MVI are listed in Table I. Though the vitamin D content (400 IU) is half the dose associated with decreased  stress  fractures  among  navy  recruits  reported  by Lappe et al., 28 the 27 mg of iron approximates the estimated 22 mg daily requirement for females in military training. 8
A study by Barnes et al. 35 retrospectively investigated the effects of prescribing this MVI to female trainees and 'found a  statistically  nonsignificant  effect  of  prenatal  vitamin  supplementation on attrition from training and on development of stress fractures and iron deficiency anemia among females undergoing U.S. Air Force BMT' but deemed the 26% associated reduction in medical attrition as 'operationally adequate to justify continuation' of the program. Those authors noted limitations from its nonrandomized, retrospective nature comparing trainees who were prescribed the prenatal and counseled  on  its  potential  benefits  and  risks  with  a  historical season-matched  control  group  that  previously  matriculated BMT and lack of assessment of compliance. A 2014 survey of female BMT trainees found that less than half reported daily MVI compliance. 35
